Economic.description: Strategies that manipulate cost structures, market incentives, or economic asymmetries to entrench dominance.

strategies.name: Data Network Effects
strategies.definition: A feedback loop where user activity improves the system’s intelligence, making the platform increasingly indispensable.
strategies.mechanism: Usage → data accumulation → improved performance → more usage.

strategies.name: Loss-Leader Infrastructure
strategies.definition: Offering core infrastructure or compute below cost to absorb workloads and later monetize the captive user base.

strategies.name: Regulatory Arbitrage
strategies.definition: Exploiting jurisdictional or temporal differences in regulations to gain early market advantage.
strategies.mechanism: Operate in gray zones before compliance catches up.

Technical.description: Strategies that leverage engineering, protocols, and infrastructure design to create structural dependency.

strategies.name: Algorithmic Opacity
strategies.definition: Hiding algorithmic logic, model weights, or decision criteria to maintain control over outputs and distribution.
strategies.mechanism: Information asymmetry as a power tool.

strategies.name: Ecosystem Envelopment
strategies.definition: Expanding into complementary layers, converting them into controlled dependencies.

strategies.name: Continuous Integration Drift
strategies.definition: Silent version drift in APIs or SDKs that breaks compatibility without explicit version changes.

strategies.name: Standard Capture
strategies.definition: Influencing or dominating standards bodies to shape ‘open’ protocols that favor proprietary ecosystems.

strategies.name: Strategic Interoperability
strategies.definition: Allowing partial interoperability to attract users while maintaining ultimate dependency barriers.

Cognitive.description: Strategies that exploit human, social, or organizational biases to generate self-reinforcing adoption.

strategies.name: Ecosystem Gravity
strategies.definition: Lock-in through identity, reputation, and social context rather than functionality.
strategies.mechanism: Community and habit as retention levers.

strategies.name: Information Asymmetry Control
strategies.definition: Managing perception by selectively disclosing or redefining metrics, shaping external narratives.
strategies.mechanism: Signal control to steer regulators or investors.

meta.summary: These 10 strategies operate across economic, technical, and cognitive axes. Together they form the modern 'ecosystemic competition' model, where control over data, interfaces, and perception replaces direct price or product competition.
